title: Design a useful card stand
outcome: CONSTRUCTION: design a product to solve a problem.
goal: I can plan a useful card stand, show three ideas and explain my choice.
success: I can turn a small problem into clear design checks.
I can sketch three different ideas and add useful labels.
I can choose one idea and give reasons linked to the brief.
purpose: Invented client Sam uses one paper prompt card at a desk. The card is 80 mm wide and 60 mm high. It falls flat, so Sam cannot read it while working. Design a small tabletop stand to keep the card upright and easy to read. It must hold the card for 30 seconds with hands away on a level table. Keep the message clear and let the card be removed by hand. The whole stand, including its channel, must fit a 160 mm wide by 120 mm deep table area. It must have safe edges and no loose sharp parts.
specification: Holds one 80 mm wide by 60 mm high paper card without hiding its message.
Try the actual card after making; check fit and message view.
Holds the card for 30 seconds with hands away on a level table.
After adult clearance, place the actual card in the stand on a level table; hands away for 30 seconds.
Easy to move, with safe edges and no loose sharp parts.
Adult checks edges and joins before a gentle handling test.
Fits a 160 mm by 120 mm table area including the channel; possible with agreed hand tools.
Adult reviews size, material, joining and safe access before making.
idea_prompts: A folded strip makes a triangular stand with a U-shaped retaining channel. Label the base, support and channel.
A broad slot base holds an upright backplate. How will it grip or support the thin paper card? Label the slot and back.
A back panel supports the card. Side braces help it stay upright. Label the back, braces and card rest.
model_choice: Adult model only: I would explore a folded triangular stand because a broad base could help it stand on the desk. A shallow U-shaped channel could catch the lower edge of the card. I still need to check the card fit, material and join before making. This is a prediction, not a passed test. Your three ideas and final reason must be your own.
dimensions: The prompt card is 80 mm wide and 60 mm high. Label the card size. The default triangular body has a 120 mm wide by 80 mm deep base. Its U-shaped channel projects beyond the front; allow a 160 mm by 120 mm table area for the whole stand. Label a sensible proposed stand size in mm; the adult reviews any changed design before Week 2. A sketch is not a cutting template. Written measurements and the actual approved plan govern later cutting.
safety: This is a design lesson. Drawing, speaking, signing or pupil-directed scribing can meet today's task. No cutting, hot glue or powered equipment is needed.
Use hand tools only in this block, and only when the adult approves the actual task and supervision. Do not collect or try tools on your own.
Before any later cutting or joining, the adult checks the material, tool, work area, grip and safe route. An approved design is not tool permission.
For a concern or pause, stop, put any tool down in its agreed place and tell the adult. Restart only after the adult has made the task safe.
A drawing or empty-hand model is planning evidence. It does not prove that a stand has been made, tested or found safe.
fallback: With no card, paper, ruler, printer or tools, hear the brief and picture three different stand shapes. Describe each one and two useful labels, by speech or signing. Choose one with a reason linked to Sam's problem. An adult records exact confirmed words when a recording method is available; mark transcription pending until it exists. Keep physical sketches, measuring, making and product tests pending where not done.
careers: Product designers turn a user's small problem into a clear brief. They compare ideas and explain why a design may work before a maker cuts material.

stages.name: Arrival
stages.title: A card that falls flat
pupil: Meet Sam, an invented client.
One 80 mm by 60 mm card falls flat on the desk.
We will design a stand to hold it upright.
stages.teacher: Read the invented brief. Show or describe a paper card 80 mm wide by 60 mm high. Demonstrate it lying flat without asking for personal possessions or difficulties. Ask what Sam needs to read and why the stand must hold itself up. Today is planning; no cutting or joining is required. Use the last minute for a calm settling pause.
stages.check: Ask: What is the problem? Expect the card falls flat and is hard to read while working. Re-read the brief if the answer only names decoration.

stages.name: Starter
stages.title: What must a useful stand do
pupil: Hold the card upright.
Stand on its own on the desk.
Keep the message clear and edges safe.
stages.teacher: Turn the need into three short checks: card fit and message view, stability, safe handling. Explain that a specification is a list of checks a design must meet. It describes success, not a made product result. Ask the pupil for one useful check in their own words.
stages.check: Ask which is easier to check later: looks nice or stands on its own with the card. Expect the second; ask how they could check it after making.

stages.name: I do
stages.title: Model one annotated idea
pupil: A quick sketch can show a shape.
Add labels for what each part does.
Link a feature to a design check.
stages.teacher: Think aloud one folded-stand idea. Draw a base, sloping support and U-shaped retaining channel; label the 80 by 60 mm card. Add: wide base may help it stand; U channel may catch the card edge. Use may because the unmade design has not been tested. Model one reason, then fade the final label to a pupil suggestion. Do not present the model as the pupil's work or only acceptable design.
stages.check: Ask what makes a label useful. Expect it names a part and says how it helps, such as base helps the stand stay upright. A neat outline without explanation is not enough.

stages.name: We do
stages.title: Compare different ways to solve it
pupil: Compare a triangle, slot base and braced back.
What supports the card in each idea?
Name one possible strength and one question.
stages.teacher: Use three quick shape prompts. A folded triangle has a broad base; a slot base and backplate need a grip that suits the actual thin card; a braced back needs secure joins and a card rest. These are starting points, not tested products. Pupils can change a shape or suggest another. Compare against the same checks. Use property, feature, effect as short spoken chunks. Plan in any language.
stages.check: Ask the pupil to point to a different support feature in two ideas. If they repeat only the colour, re-point to base, slot or brace and ask how it supports the card.

stages.name: We do 2
stages.title: Does the reason solve the problem
pupil: A stand is blue, so it must hold the card upright. Is that enough?
Choose yes, no, or only if it looks neat.
Explain which feature needs checking.
stages.teacher: Hinge answer is no. Colour alone does not show card support or stability. Re-point to the brief, then model: a broad base may help it stand on its own. Parallel check: a sketch shows a U channel; has the actual card passed a slip test? No, the design predicts an effect but the made stand must be tested later. Recheck after a brief reteach.
stages.check: Move on when the pupil links a feature to the problem and separates a design prediction from an actual test. If not, choose Supported and compare two feature labels with adult-led prompts.

stages.name: Independent
stages.title: Three ideas and my own choice
pupil: In your book, write three clear design checks.
Make three quick different sketches. Add two useful labels to each.
Choose one idea. Give two reasons linked to your checks.
Keep a question or change for the next maker.
stages.teacher: Use one route. Suggest about three minutes for quick sketches, two for labels, two for choosing and one to check. Sketches can be rough; record real features and purposes. With access support, the pupil may direct sketches or describe three distinct ideas and confirm a scribe's record. Do not reduce the three-idea requirement. The pupil may choose a taught starting point but must own the choice and reasons.
stages.check: Check three distinct ideas, two useful labels per idea, three checkable design points, a selected idea and two purpose-linked reasons. Check card dimensions and any proposed stand size; do not invent a measurement or completed test.

stages.name: Review
stages.title: Check the choice against the brief
pupil: Does your chosen idea support the card?
Can you explain the base, card rest and safe handling?
Improve one label or reason.
stages.teacher: Offer a private adult review, or a peer comment only by consent. Check the choice against the specification rather than awarding a test pass. Let the pupil change a label, shape or reason and record why. The adult notes any design or tool questions for Week 2. Use the last minute to organise books and return any demonstration item.
stages.check: Pupil confirms their final idea and scribed words. Record the actual page and support. If a key design point is missing, mark it to complete before a cutting list is approved.

stages.name: Exit
stages.title: A reason for the next maker
pupil: My chosen idea is ___.
It could help Sam because ___.
Next week I need to check ___.
stages.teacher: Ask for a short own-word choice and reason, privately if preferred. Keep the actual brief, specification, three ideas and decision for Week 2. Name the build-planning step without starting it. Unfinished planning stays honestly marked.
stages.check: Evidence is the pupil's specification, three annotated ideas and chosen design with reasons, actual date, location and support. It is not proof of making or testing. Record only what happened.

Supported: Hear the brief and choose three design checks from the prompt list.
Use the three shape prompts. Make three quick different sketches, or direct an adult to draw them.
Point, say or sign two useful labels for each idea. Name what each part does.
Choose one idea. Give two short reasons. Confirm your own words and one question.
Standard: Write three clear design checks for Sam's stand.
Sketch three different ideas and give each two labels about its features and jobs.
Choose one idea and explain two links to your design checks.
Add the 80 mm by 60 mm card size, a proposed stand size and one question to check next week.
Stretch: Complete the three ideas, labels and final choice first.
Compare your chosen idea with one rejected idea against the same checks.
Explain a trade-off, such as a broad base using more card but helping stability.
Propose a fair later test. Separate a prediction from an actual result.

vocabulary: The person who needs the product. Sam is invented.
The problem and the useful job the product must do.
A list of checks the design must meet.
Add short labels that explain a part or its job.
How well an item stays standing in its planned use.
A gain in one feature that may bring a limit in another.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Read one design check at a time. Use three simple shape prompts and a repeated part, job, reason frame. Keep card dimensions visible. Fade a model to labels, then to an own-word choice.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Accept pointing, speech, signing and pupil-directed scribing or drawing. Give thinking time and a choice before an open question. Read every final idea and reason back for correction.
adaptations.SEMH: Keep the client and problem invented. No personal possessions or difficulties need to be shown. Offer private review and a calm pause. Put any tools down first and agree a safe return.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Use a large diagram, a spoken shape description or adult drawing directed by the pupil. Do not force handling. Plan later grip, cutting and joining support before any practical tool use.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Pair client, brief and base words with a simple sketch or gesture. Use part, job and reason as short spoken chunks. Preserve pupil meaning in confirmed scribing.
adaptations.Literacy and Numeracy: Read mm as millimetres. Keep 80 mm by 60 mm beside the card sketch. Model one short part and job label, then fade to a sentence start. Record proposed sizes clearly without treating a picture as a measured template.
